title: What the reformers asked
hookLine: grace, scripture, and real abuses; Catholics today admit many of the abuses were real

lines: FROM THE HEAD TO THE MEMBERS.
cards: A papal envoy stands before a German assembly with a message from the new pope, Adrian the Sixth. Instead of a defense, the envoy reads out a confession.

The pope's instruction admits that for years there had been grave abuses in the Holy See itself, that the sickness had spread from the head to the members, and that the pope means to begin the cure at home.
A pope, in the middle of the storm, saying: some of this is our fault. So what did the reformers ask?

teach.b: They asked three kinds of things. First, grace. Luther read Paul's letter to the Romans, which in the Douay-Rheims says, "The just man liveth by faith."
He came to believe we are made right with God by grace, received through faith, not earned.
Catholics also teach that grace comes first and can't be bought; the real disagreements were about how grace works in a person, and those took longer to sort out.
Second, scripture. The reformers wanted the Bible in ordinary people's hands and languages, and held it to be the final rule over every church teaching.
Catholics hold scripture and tradition together, read within the Church. That disagreement is real, and it's still discussed.
Third, the abuses, where the reformers were often simply right. Some bishops drew income from dioceses they rarely saw. Church offices were bought and sold.
Some priests had barely been taught. And indulgences had been marketed like a product.
Pope Adrian's instruction said as much, and so did Catholic reformers inside the Church, before and after Luther. Then, why it matters.

You can disagree with the reformers about grace or scripture and still say plainly: they saw real wounds. The Second Vatican Council said that for the separations, often enough, people on both sides were to blame.
Honest reform can start with that kind of admission.

how: Catholic and Protestant theologians continue to discuss grace, scripture and authority in formal dialogues; Catholic leaders have publicly acknowledged that abuses in the Church of that era were real.

o: the pope who confessed abuses in the Holy See
a Catholic reformer who led the Council of Trent
the reformer who read Paul on grace and named abuses

games.q: you're a new pope. a reform movement is tearing the West apart, and some of its complaints about Rome are true. what do you send?
o: a flat denial of every charge.
an admission that the sickness began at the head, and a promise to cure it at home.
games.why: Adrian VI's instruction admitted grave abuses in the Holy See and said the cure would begin there.

practice: Let your week pass before you, what you said, what you spent, how you treated the people closest to you, and look for one habit in you that's drifted, the way an office drifts into a privilege.
Don't fix it yet; just name it in one honest sentence, the way Pope Adrian's letter named the abuses. If you pray, bring that sentence before God.

wordCard.voice: Luther. The reformer who read Paul on grace, called for scripture in everyone's hands, and pointed to abuses the Church needed to face. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the abuses were real. Hearing the true part of a criticism is where honest reform begins. Day seven hundred eighty-two, done.
